Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a step‑by‑step outline of how I would use the two tools you described to place an order for a burger and fries at McDonald’s. I’ll keep it high‑level so you can see the logical flow without getting bogged down in implementation details. --- ## 1. Discover the Ordering API | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **1.1** | **Search** the web for “McDonald’s online ordering API” or “McDonald’s digital menu API”. | We need to know whether McDonald’s exposes a public API (or a partner API) that lets us programmatically fetch menu data and submit orders. | | **1.2** | **Identify** the relevant endpoints:
• `/menu` – returns the full menu hierarchy.
• `/order` – accepts new orders.
• `/order/{id}` – checks status. | Knowing the exact URLs and HTTP verbs lets us construct the correct calls later. | | **1.3** | **Collect** any required headers, query parameters, or authentication mechanisms (OAuth token, API key, etc.). | Without the right auth we won’t be able to reach the endpoints. | --- ## 2. Gather Menu Information | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **2.1** | **Execute** a `GET /menu` call (using the “execute API call” tool). | We need the current menu structure to locate the exact product IDs for a burger and fries. | | **2.2** | **Parse** the JSON response to find:
• The category “Burgers” (or similar).
• The specific item “Big Mac” (or whatever burger you want).
• The fries item (“Regular Fries”). | The API will likely return a nested list of categories → items. We need the numeric IDs that the order endpoint expects. | | **2.3** | **Store** the IDs (e.g., `burger_id = 12345`, `fries_id = 67890`). | These IDs will be inserted into the order payload. | --- ## 3. Build the Order Payload | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **3.1** | **Create** a JSON object that matches the schema expected by `/order`. Typical fields:
• `location_id` – your nearest McDonald’s store.
• `items` – array of `{product_id, quantity}`.
• `payment_method` – e.g., `"card"` with tokenized card info.
• `delivery_address` – if delivery; otherwise set to “pickup”. | The order endpoint will validate the payload against this schema. | | **3.2** | **Populate** the fields:
• `location_id` – look up the nearest store via a separate endpoint or a static lookup.
• `items`: `[{"product_id": burger_id, "quantity": 1}, {"product_id": fries_id, "quantity": 1}]`.
• `payment_method`: use a test token or a real card token if you’re actually paying.
• `delivery_address`: set to your address or leave empty for pickup. | This is the meat of the order. | | **3.3** | **Validate** the JSON against the schema (if you have a validator). | Prevents malformed requests that would fail outright. | --- ## 4. Submit the Order | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **4.1** | **Execute** a `POST /order` call with the payload built in step 3. | This is the action that creates the order in McDonald’s system. | | **4.2** | **Handle** the response:
• Success → contains `order_id`, estimated preparation time, etc.
• Failure → error code/message (e.g., “invalid payment”, “item out of stock”). | We need to know whether the order was accepted and what to do next. | | **4.3** | **Store** the `order_id` for future status checks. | The order ID is required to poll for updates. | --- ## 5. Confirm & Track the Order | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **5.1** | **Send** a confirmation to the user (you or the customer) with the order ID and ETA. | Keeps the user informed. | | **5.2** | **Poll** `/order/{order_id}` periodically (e.g., every 30 seconds) until the status changes to “ready” or “completed”. | Allows us to update the user on progress or handle cancellations. | | **5.3** | **Notify** the user when the order is ready for pickup or has been delivered. | Completes the ordering loop. | --- ## 6. Error Handling & Retries | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **6.1** | **Detect** transient errors (HTTP 5xx, network timeouts). | These may succeed on retry. | | **6.2** | **Retry** the failed request up to 3 times with exponential back‑off. | Improves reliability. | | **6.3** | **Escalate** permanent failures (HTTP 4xx, invalid payload) to human support or log them for debugging. | Ensures we don’t silently fail. | --- ## 7. Optional Enhancements | Feature | How to add it | Benefit | |---------|---------------|---------| | **Dynamic location** | Call a geocoding API to convert the user’s address into a `location_id`. | Orders can be placed at the nearest store automatically. | | **Promotions** | Query a `/promotions` endpoint and apply discount codes to the order payload. | Saves money for the customer. | | **Order history** | Store past `order_id`s in a database and expose a `/history` endpoint. | Lets users re‑order quickly. | --- ### Summary Flow ``` search() → identify endpoints → execute GET /menu → parse IDs → build order JSON → execute POST /order → confirm → poll status → notify user ``` By following this sequence—discovering the API, fetching menu data, constructing a valid order payload, submitting it, and tracking the result—you can reliably place a burger and fries order at McDonald’s using the two tools you mentioned.
